# Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite

Jonno,

Right. Here’s what happened with the coolroom. You can stop messaging me now. Some of us still work in a kitchen instead of moving to London and getting soft.

You would’ve cried. I want that established before we get into it. You’ll say you wouldn’t have, but I worked grill next to you. I know what you’re like when a tea towel’s slightly damp.

Cup Day. Tuesday, 3 November. I get in at 6.40am and the coolroom thermometer says 11 degrees.

Eleven.

Not a coolroom temperature. More of a pleasant London afternoon. You’d probably have your shirt off in a park.

The compressor had died overnight, which was thoughtful timing considering we had 140 booked for lunch. Set menu. Three courses. Raff was away, so I was running it. All I needed was a functioning kitchen, and apparently that was getting a bit ambitious.

Called Wally from Coldline. Wally couldn’t come until Wednesday. Part coming from Sydney.

I have no personal issue with Sydney, but it’s a fucking long way from a compressor you need working before lunch.

Phil’s contribution was, “Just make it work mate.”

Good stuff, Phil. I’d been considering not making it work, but that opened up a whole new avenue.

You remember how owners say that like they’ve given you instructions? Like you can put “make it work” on the prep list, somewhere between pick shallots and portion beef. No worries mate, how many litres of work would you like made?

Anyway. We started finding fridge space.

Both undercounters. The bar fridge. Then Marta next door let us use half her walk-in, which is the reason I’m writing a blog post about this instead of standing in the laneway screaming.

There is nothing quite like suddenly needing to fit a coolroom’s worth of things into places that already have things in them. You spend all year telling people not to cram the undercounters, then one Tuesday morning you’re looking at a bar fridge with the intensity of a bloke defusing a bomb.

Lost about $1,800 in stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs.

The duck legs hurt. I won’t give them a big memorial here, but you know.

While all this was happening, Benny and I had to get 30 kilos of beef shin down the laneway to Marta’s. In the rain. On a milk crate trolley.

One wheel fell off.

Of course it did. Couldn’t have fallen off on a quiet Thursday while someone was moving a carton of napkins. Had to wait until it had a meaningful role in the business.

So there’s me and Benny, wet as shit, trying to move 30 kilos of beef with a trolley that had resigned halfway through the job.

That’s the bit you saw on my story. I appreciate that your response, from the other side of the world, was to ask what the fuck we were doing. Very useful. Should’ve put you on speaker with Phil. Between “what the fuck are you doing” and “just make it work mate” we could’ve had a full management meeting.

Meanwhile Kev had got the old esky and gone to the servo for ice.

Fourteen bags.

Servo bloke asked if we were having a party.

I keep thinking about what sort of party Kev looked like he was preparing for. Fourteen bags of servo ice on Cup morning. Fair question, really. Less festive when you find out the guest of honour is dairy.

And then lunch happened.

That’s the stupid part. After all that, we still had to do the actual job. Nobody books a three-course lunch because they want to hear about your refrigeration. You can’t walk out and tell 140 people you’ve already had quite a big morning and would they mind sorting themselves out.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”, which isn’t wording I’d recommend spending money getting printed on a menu, but there we were.

People loved it.

Possibly more than they would’ve loved the panna cotta.

I’m choosing not to examine that too closely. You can spend ages getting a dessert right, or you can have a mechanical failure and give people coffee and whatever’s left. Apparently both are valid approaches. One involves considerably more phone calls to Wally.

Then a lady on table nine asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway”.

She’d seen us out the window.

Can’t even be angry. That’s good. She’d watched two idiots escort her lunch through the rain on a broken trolley and waited until she had an audience. Fair play to her.

You would’ve been unbearable about that. We’d still be hearing it in March. Every beef order: “Is that the laneway one?” Every delivery: “Let them roam, chef.” I know exactly how much mileage you’d get out of it because you once found something funny and made it everyone’s problem for six months.

The annoying thing is, I reckon it was the best service we’ve done all year.

Not saying we should kill the coolroom before every big booking. I’d prefer to try having all our equipment working and see how that feels.

But everyone was locked in. There was too much to do for anyone to get carried away with their own bullshit. Kev sorted the ice. Benny was right there with me. We had stock spread between our kitchen, the bar and next door, and somehow we got through 140 covers and people had a good lunch.

I’d have loved you on grill. Even allowing for the crying.

Marta, meanwhile, has established repayment terms. Croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal, which seems fair until you remember she’s now got leverage over me and knows exactly how desperate I was.

She earned it. Half her walk-in on Cup Day. Absolute legend. I’ll feed her for as long as she wants, although I’d appreciate a written date at which the debt is considered settled.

And my horse in the sweep?

Ice Cold Lad.

Came second last.

After spending the day trying to keep a bistro cold with borrowed fridge space and fourteen bags of ice, I had actual money on something called Ice Cold Lad. The universe is taking the piss and it’s not even being subtle.

So that was Cup Day. Eighteen hundred bucks in the bin, a wheel off the trolley, no panna cotta, and somehow a service I’m genuinely pretty happy with.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. You knew that before you went overseas and became delicate.

Come home ya flog.
